section_summary: The section opens with the conclusion of a Spanish-language work on the Far East, reproducing provisions of the League Covenant and treaties involving China, Japan, Germany, and the Soviet Union. The remainder consists chiefly of State Department records from 1932–1934 concerning reported Japanese arms sales, military advisers, aviation activity, propaganda, immigration, commercial expansion, and possible strategic footholds in Peru during and after the Leticia dispute. Later reports assess the large Japanese community, agricultural and commercial penetration, Peruvian opposition and immigration restrictions, and the largely unverified rumors of naval bases, warship purchases, and Japanese plans against the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: El drama del Extremo Oriente: Covenant and treaty extracts, conclusion
subfiles.about: Concludes a Spanish-language compilation of international agreements bearing on East Asian affairs.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt completes provisions of the League Covenant concerning arbitration, collective security, and sanctions. It then reproduces the Shandong clauses of the Treaty of Versailles, the Nine-Power Treaty on China, the 1924 Sino-Soviet agreement, and the 1925 Soviet-Japanese convention. The final texts address Chinese sovereignty, the open-door principle, Outer Mongolia, the Chinese Eastern Railway, extraterritoriality, and mutual promises against subversive activity.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Lima Despatch No. 2452
subfiles.about: Summarizes a press report alleging that Japanese activity in Peru could threaten the Panama Canal and the Pacific coast.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum digests Lima Despatch No. 2452 and its enclosed article, “Imperial Japan's Maneuvers in Peru.” It highlights stories of Peruvian arms purchases and claims that Japanese rights at Callao or in the Galápagos Islands could threaten the Panama Canal and the coast from Chile to Panama.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2452 transmitting an El Telégrafo article
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, United States Ambassador in Lima
subfiles.about: Transmits a Guayaquil newspaper article depicting Japanese activities in Peru as a possible basis for conflict with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Dearing encloses a clipping and translation from El Telégrafo of December 16, 1932. He explains that Colombian and Ecuadorian newspapers were portraying Japanese economic penetration and colonization in Peru as preparations for action against the United States in a future war.

subfiles.title: “El Imperio del Japón maniobra en el Perú”
subfiles.about: Argues that Japanese arms dealings and strategic interests in Peru could endanger the Panama Canal and the western coast of the Americas.
subfiles.summary: The article repeats reports that Japanese pilots were operating over the upper Amazon and that Peru sought to exchange guano for Japanese arms during the Leticia crisis. It speculates that Callao and the Galápagos Islands could become strategic centers for the Japanese Navy in a future conflict with the United States. The author urges Ibero-American countries to consider the implications of Japanese expansion.

subfiles.title: Translation of “Imperial Japan's Manoeuvres in Peru”
subfiles.about: Provides the English translation of the El Telégrafo article on alleged Japanese strategic and military designs in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The translation describes reports of Japanese aviators, Peruvian purchases of Japanese arms, and a proposed exchange of guano for rifles. It presents Callao and the Galápagos as possible bases threatening the Panama Canal and the American Pacific coast. It also discusses Japanese economic interests in Peru and possible expansion in Brazil and elsewhere in Latin America.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Bogotá Despatch No. 5022
subfiles.about: Points to a Colombian despatch reporting Japanese engineers assisting Peruvian forces in mining the Amazon River.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Despatch No. 5022 from Colombia under the Japanese military-activity file. Its specific subject is the report that Peruvian forces at Leticia were placing mines in the Amazon with Japanese assistance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5022 on Colombian naval and air forces
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, for the United States Minister in Bogotá
subfiles.about: Reports Colombian expeditionary movements and a claim that Japanese engineers were helping Peru mine the Amazon near Leticia.
subfiles.summary: The despatch records the arrival at Manaus of vessels belonging to General Alfredo Vásquez Cobo's Colombian Amazon expedition and plans to coordinate river and air operations. It also reviews Colombian purchases of ships and aircraft and clarifies President Olaya's account of those acquisitions. Foreign Minister Roberto Urdaneta Arbeláez showed Dawson a telegram alleging that Japanese engineers were assisting Peruvian forces in placing mines in the Amazon River.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Bogotá Despatch No. 5080
subfiles.about: References a Colombian despatch reporting the employment of Japanese aviators by Peru.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs researchers to Despatch No. 5080 from Dawson in Colombia. It files the document under reports that Peru employed Japanese aviators.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5080 on Leticia military information
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, for the United States Minister in Bogotá
subfiles.about: Reports the progress of Colombia's Amazon flotilla and rumors that Japanese aviators had joined Peruvian service.
subfiles.summary: President Olaya reported that General Vásquez Cobo's flotilla was advancing toward Leticia, though slowly, while other Colombian vessels faced delays and possible crew disaffection. The despatch also refers to a German aviator connected with Peruvian aviation and repeats a Lima press report that two Japanese aviators had participated in Peruvian Army maneuvers near Chorrillos.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 5312
subfiles.from: United States Legation in Colombia; Jefferson Caffery
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting three high-ranking Japanese officers traveling to Peru.
subfiles.summary: The filing sheet points to Despatch No. 5312 from Colombia. Its stated subject is a Colombian Government telegram concerning three high-ranking Japanese officers en route to Peru.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for War Department letter
subfiles.about: References a War Department letter on Japanese armament and munitions assistance to Peru during the Leticia dispute.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a War Department communication concerning Japanese military activity in Peru. It characterizes the subject as Japan's supply of armament and munitions to Peru during the Leticia dispute.

subfiles.title: Panama Canal Department transmittal and G-2 endorsement
subfiles.from: Charles R. Finley; H. H. Laughlin
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff for Military Intelligence; Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Transmits Carleton Beals's report on Japanese activity in Peru and records a G-2 assessment of it.
subfiles.summary: Major Charles R. Finley forwarded a letter from Peru by the writer Carleton Beals as potentially useful intelligence. An April 18 endorsement by H. H. Laughlin judged the report generally correct but described it as further confirmation rather than new information.

subfiles.title: Carleton Beals letter on Japanese activity in Peru
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese immigration, economic organization, propaganda, arms dealings, and settlement in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Beals describes favored Japanese immigration, cooperative control of Japanese businesses, a newspaper and school, trade missions, and propaganda claiming kinship between Japanese and Incas. He reports an exchange of guano for military equipment, rumors of battleship construction, and a concentrated Japanese settlement near Chimbote. He also notes APRA hostility, an uncorroborated claim that Japanese residents might resist Apristas by force, and the lack of firm evidence that Japanese officers trained Peruvian troops.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 649 forwarding the Beals report
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Fred Morris Dearing, American Ambassador in Lima
subfiles.about: Requests confidential Embassy comment on Carleton Beals's account of Japanese immigration and commercial predominance in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the Panama Canal Department communication and Beals's March 25 letter. It asks Dearing to comment particularly on continued Japanese immigration, Japanese influence in retail and wholesale trade, and settlements near Chimbote.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3392, “Japanese Activity in Peru”
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., for the Ambassador in Lima
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese public diplomacy in Lima and rumors of Japanese naval, aviation, and military aid to Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy transmits a Japanese Legation statement published in El Comercio's special Japanese edition on the Emperor's birthday and describes associated receptions, athletics, advertising, and publicity. It identifies Saburō Kurusu as an important organizer of closer Peruvian-Japanese relations. The Consulate General had also heard rumors of five submarines, five destroyers, additional war matériel, Japanese aviators, three Japanese Army officers, and extensive Japanese credit for Peruvian purchases.

subfiles.title: “La política internacional del Japón”
subfiles.about: Presents Japan's official case for peaceful cooperation, an Asian regional doctrine, and closer economic relations with the Americas and Peru.
subfiles.summary: The clipping portrays Japanese foreign policy as peaceful and cooperative despite withdrawal from the League of Nations. It invokes Japanese special interests in China and an Asian counterpart to the Monroe Doctrine while emphasizing historical, cultural, and commercial ties across the Pacific. Adjacent newspaper material concerns members of the Japanese imperial family.

subfiles.title: Translation of “The International Policy of Japan”
subfiles.about: Translates the Japanese Legation's statement advocating peaceful political, cultural, and commercial cooperation with Peru and the Americas.
subfiles.summary: The statement presents the Pacific as a peaceful link between Japan and the American continents and recalls Peru's establishment of relations with Japan in 1873. It argues that bilateral trade remained small but was growing rapidly, especially in Peruvian raw materials and Japanese manufactured goods. It defends the Japanese colony as industrious and beneficial and defines Japanese policy as friendship, useful employment of residents, and mutual prosperity.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3394 on Peru's reported purchase of munitions
subfiles.about: Reports claims that Japan would finance Peruvian warships in return for mineral rights and a munitions factory concession.
subfiles.summary: The confidential source alleged that Peru would receive five submarines and five destroyers against a Japanese credit of 100 million soles. In return, Japan would obtain ten-year rights to southern Peruvian iron deposits and a concession for a gun and ammunition factory. The despatch also repeats rumors involving the Galápagos, Japanese aviators, ammunition in Junín, and powerful machine guns, while warning that Japanese agents were actively seeking raw materials and government business along South America's west coast.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ambassador Grew concerning Japanese activity in Peru
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests discreet information on reports of Japanese warship sales, mineral concessions, aviators, and resource acquisition in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses Lima Despatch No. 3394 for Grew's information. Without making a specific inquiry, the Tokyo Embassy was to seek information bearing on the reported naval deal, iron rights, munitions factory, Japanese aviators, and Japanese pursuit of South American raw materials.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3400 on proposed Japanese control of the Peruvian Steamship Company
subfiles.about: Describes negotiations that might give Japanese interests control of the Peruvian Steamship Company in return for drydock assistance.
subfiles.summary: Japanese interests were negotiating with the financially troubled Compañía Peruana de Vapores while the Peruvian Government urgently sought a drydock. Dearing explains that control of the vessels could help distribute Japanese goods, collect exports, dominate coastwise trade under Peruvian registry, and weaken immigration restrictions. The company's president preferred assistance from Grace & Company, which was referring the strategic and commercial implications to its New York office and United States agencies.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Despatch No. 3400 to Tokyo
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the Lima report on Japanese efforts to control the Peruvian Steamship Company.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends Ambassador Grew a confidential copy of Despatch No. 3400. The instruction identifies the attempted Japanese acquisition of control over the Peruvian Steamship Company as the report's central subject.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on the reported lease of Asia Island
subfiles.about: References a report that Peru leased the guano island of Asia to Japan for ninety-nine years.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Lima Despatch No. 3221. It records a statement that Asia Island, north of Cerro Azul, had been placed at Japan's disposal for any uses Japan considered convenient.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 3410
subfiles.about: References a report on Japanese munitions representatives Seigo Oguni and Taro Yuasa and Japanese trade efforts in South America.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs the file to Despatch No. 3410. It identifies Japanese munitions activity and broader efforts to improve trade relations with South America as relevant to the military-activity file.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3410 excerpt on military conditions and Japanese activity
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., for the Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: Reviews Peruvian preparations against Colombia and Ecuador and the arrival of Japanese munitions sellers in Lima.
subfiles.summary: The report discusses Peruvian troop and supply planning for Loreto, airfield construction near Chiclayo and toward Iquitos, and preparations for possible hostilities with Colombia or Ecuador. It says a Japanese munitions commission included Seigo Oguni and Major Taro Yuasa. The Embassy interpreted the mission as part of Japan's effort to sell surplus goods and obtain iron, cotton, copper, sugar, petroleum, and other raw materials along South America's west coast.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Tokyo Despatch No. 859
subfiles.about: References a discussion with Dr. Esguerra about Japanese efforts to gain a strategic and military foothold in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Tokyo Despatch No. 859. Its subject is Ambassador Grew's conversation with Colombia's first minister to Japan concerning Japanese efforts to establish a strategically and militarily useful position in Peru.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the status of Japanese penetration in Peru
subfiles.from: S. E. Grummon, Division of Latin-American Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Despatch No. 3634 on Japanese population, business ownership, agricultural settlement, opposition, and trade in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates approximately 50,000 Japanese in Peru and notes the recent denunciation of the 1924 commercial treaty that had allowed unrestricted immigration. It gives examples of Japanese ownership in Lima, Chimbote, and the Chanchamayo Valley, while describing growing press, labor-law, and popular opposition. Trade figures show a sharp rise in Japanese exports to Peru between 1932 and 1934.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3634, “Japanese Penetration in Peru”
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, United States Ambassador in Lima
subfiles.about: Provides an extensive assessment of Japanese immigration, commerce, agriculture, propaganda, military contacts, and political influence in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Dearing agrees that Japanese penetration was rapid and organized but considers its immediate motivation primarily demographic and commercial, while declining to dismiss possible strategic designs against the Panama Canal. He traces Japanese immigration, official and cooperative support, the 1924 treaty, schools and newspapers, the Inca-Japanese kinship campaign, and mounting Peruvian opposition represented by APRA, agrarian interests, the press, and the 80-percent employment laws. Detailed sections describe Japanese agricultural colonies and urban businesses, visits by commercial, athletic, artistic, and military missions, and Peru's wartime purchasing mission to Japan during the Leticia dispute. The surviving portion ends amid an examination of arms purchased with guano, rejecting the largest estimates and treating reported Japanese warship sales as unsubstantiated.
